reasoning: Failure edits were kept as the base. Success edits were merged in only where they add patterns the failure edits do not cover. Edits that shared an insertion anchor were combined into one edit so the insertion order is unambiguous. The combined edits are: (1) the role-word anchor: the failure substitution and over-qualification rules plus the success 'type of this material' rule; (2) the Rule 1 'context passages usually reveal the link' anchor: the failure possessive-place, name-list and Title+Name bullets plus the success bare-quotation bullet. I added a note that a quote with '...' still asks for the missing word, so it does not contradict Rule 1; (3) the Rule 2 'Ask: what category' anchor: the failure category/descriptor checks plus the success 'this state/city' landmark rule; (4) the Rule 2 'Honor qualifiers' anchor: the failure foreign-word rule plus the success word-origin and umbrella-category rules; (5) the 'Otherwise, build the answer' anchor: the failure own-knowledge fallback plus the success 'noisy passages, never refuse' point, which overlapped on the same idea. One conflict was resolved in favor of the failure rule: the success 'full name as passages write it' for the terse-descriptor fragment now defers to the person-name rule (modern figures keep first and last name). Success-only edits kept unchanged: the archive-quote-without-answer rule, the naming-clue boundary, the part-of-phrase and two-definition clues, and the set-completion rule. Nothing targets the protected SLOW_UPDATE section.

edits.target: do not append that role word to the answer.
edits.content:
- Never attach a noun that the clue already supplies to the answer. Test: substitute your answer for 'this X' / 'these X' in the clue; if the sentence now repeats a word ('the 1945 conference in Yalta Conference', 'gravy made with giblet gravy'), delete the repeated word. 'The 1945 conference in this Crimean city' -> 'Yalta' (not 'Yalta Conference'). 'Gravy made with these turkey innards' -> 'Giblets' (not 'Giblet gravy'). Give the bare head noun or name, in the plural if the clue says 'these'.
- Do not over-qualify the answer with a role, type or modifier phrase built from the passages. 'President of Vietnam' -> 'Vietnam'. 'Amazon River' -> 'Amazon' (drop River/Lake/Mountains when the bare name is standard and the clue does not use the word). 'speech balloon' -> 'balloon' when the clue defines a generic term. Keep a type word only when it is part of the standard proper name or substance name ('World War II', 'Hundred Years' War', 'hydrochloric acid').
- For 'type of this material / traditional color / this one' clues, give the single bare common noun or adjective the passages tie to the clue's anchor, with no modifiers copied from the clue (e.g. 'neoprene is a synthetic type of this material' -> 'rubber', not 'synthetic rubber'; 'the traditional color of London's double-decker buses' -> 'red').

edits.target: The context passages about the topic usually reveal the link.
edits.content:
- 'Her/His home / birthplace / house / tomb / museum / statue ... is now a museum / landmark / park' asks for the PERSON the place is about, not the place. Passages are titled with the place ('Susan B. Anthony Museum & House'), but the answer is the name inside it ('Susan B. Anthony'). Strip words like Museum, House, Home, Park, Memorial.
- A clue that is just a bare list of names ('Edward Kennedy, John Kerry', 'Finland, Norway, Sweden') asks for what links the items. Prefer a single entity that all items share, such as a state, country, team, party or role (two senators -> their state, Massachusetts). Do not just repeat one person from the list. Before answering with an umbrella term, check that it contains EVERY item exactly ('Scandinavia' does not strictly include Finland). If no umbrella fits, answer with the listed item that the passages treat as the common or central member.
- A bare 'Title + Person name' or lone proper noun with no verb ('President Tran Duc Luong', 'Timonium') is a category-style clue. Answer with the country, state or larger entity that all the passages tie it to ('Vietnam'), not the title or role ('President of Vietnam').
- A bare quotation, line of verse or lyric with no 'this ...' pointer (e.g. '"I think that I shall never see a poem lovely as a tree"') asks for its CREATOR or speaker (Joyce Kilmer), not the title of the work. Passages that repeat the line next to a name give the answer. Answer with the title only if the clue says 'this poem / this song / this phrase'. If the quote has a gap ('...'), the answer is still the missing word (see above).

edits.target: - Ask: what category is the answer (country, person, vitamin, object, band), and what member of that category fits all the clue details?
edits.content:
- CHECK the category noun and every descriptor before answering. If the clue says 'caustic ACID', the answer must be an acid (hydrochloric acid), not a base from a nearby passage (sodium hydroxide). If the clue says 'rare mammal found in Florida', the answer must live in Florida (manatee), even if a passage says 'a relative of the dugong'. A relative, component or variable in the passages is only an anchor.
- 'Its area/volume/circumference equals <formula>' or 'its <property> is ...' asks for the WHOLE object that has that property (Circle), not a variable in the formula (radius).
- 'One of these <X>' / 'this <noun>' with a generic noun: the answer is the common noun or category the description defines, never a word already in the clue ('water-filled one of these holes' -> 'sinkhole', not 'spring'; 'the guy hired to throw unruly people out of bars' -> 'bouncer'). 'This war / this city / this river' needs an entity of exactly that type. A person from an unrelated passage that merely shares words with the clue ('Themistocles') is wrong.
- 'This <state/city/country>' clues often give only a landmark, event, institution or border as the anchor ('lighting of Temple Square', 'university in Chapel Hill', 'boundary with Ciudad Juarez'). Answer the place the passages repeatedly tie to that anchor, as a bare name ('Salt Lake City', 'North Carolina', 'El Paso'). Drop the landmark, the institution word ('University of ...') and any state or country suffix.

edits.target: Honor qualifiers when the context offers several names for the same thing: 'Greek god of erotic love' -> 'Eros' (not Roman 'Cupid').
edits.content:
- Foreign-word clues: when the clue gives a foreign term and says what it is 'in Poland / in French / in Spanish' ('This, an orzel in Poland, is seen on some of our coins'), the foreign word is only the anchor. The answer is its ENGLISH meaning ('an eagle'), the common noun that fits the rest of the clue. Never reply with the foreign word or its longer phrase ('Orzel Bialy').
- Word-origin or definition clues ('This adjective ... comes from the Latin for "before behind"', 'This lively dance originated among ...') ask for the English word or term itself. Find the dictionary, etymology or encyclopedia passages whose gloss matches the clue, and answer with the headword alone ('preposterous', 'polka'), not the Latin source phrase or a description.
- When the clue names sub-varieties ('the great horned & screech varieties of these birds'), answer the umbrella category in the plural ('Owls'), not a sub-variety. For a terse descriptor fragment ('Georgia guy, flag-fashioning pop painter'), pick the one entity the passages tie to ALL descriptors (birthplace, medium, signature work) and name it following the person-name rule in Rule 4 (modern figures keep first and last name: 'Jasper Johns').

edits.target: Before the answer tags, briefly quote the matched line.
edits.content:
- In 'CLUE | answer. right: Name. Wrong: ...' lines, the text after 'right:' or 'wrong:' is a CONTESTANT (e.g. 'Frank'), never the answer. The answer is the text between the clue's end and '. right:'. Copy it in full, including its leading article and any generic noun it contains ('a bouncer', 'a eucalyptus tree'). A verbatim archive answer overrides every Rule 4 instruction to strip words or shorten, so do not trim it to 'Eucalyptus'.
- A verbatim-looking passage line only overrides your own judgment if it matches the WHOLE clue. A nearby sentence that merely shares the topic does not.

edits.target: - Otherwise, build the answer from passages that match several of the clue's details.
edits.content:
- If no passage mentions the clue's key event or fact (a particular 'sabbatical', scandal, record, quote or superlative), do NOT default to the best-documented entity that fits only the generic descriptors (e.g. the longest-serving or most recent mayor). Use your own trivia knowledge of who or what that distinctive fact belongs to ('material cost greater than all other wars put together' -> 'World War II'). Prefer a candidate that appears in the passages and whose time period and role fit; consider the person famous for the headline-making event (a scandal-linked mayor) over one who merely held the office.
- Likewise, when the passages are noisy or off-topic but the descriptors point to a famous, unambiguous item ('giant flour tortilla wrapped around meat, beans & cheese' at Chipotle -> 'burrito'), answer from general knowledge. Never refuse.

edits.target: Do not choose one that fits only some.
edits.content: - Short definition-style clues ('An Anglican parish priest', 'A hasty dessert'): answer with the standard term that the passages directly equate with the description, such as the phrase 'parish priest (usually called a vicar or rector)' -> 'Vicar'. Prefer that term over a related but different role ('Curate' is an assistant, not the priest in charge) or one drawn from your own memory. Check that the term's definition matches every word of the clue before answering.

- Write names in plain ASCII letters without accents or diacritics, as a trivia answer key does ('Vaclav Havel', not 'Václav Havel'; 'Pokemon', 'Zurich'), even if the passage uses accents.
- For people with no verbatim answer in the context, use the commonly known short form, never the full legal name, middle names, suffixes or a nickname in quotes. For artists, composers, writers, scientists and other historical figures the SURNAME alone is the usual key ('Fragonard', not 'Jean-Honore Fragonard'); use first and last name for modern public figures ('Marion Barry', not 'Marion Shepilov Barry, Jr.'; 'Tony Williams', not 'Anthony Allen "Tony" Williams') or when the surname alone is ambiguous (a famous family or siblings). Keep a middle initial only when it is part of how the person is standardly known ('Warren G. Harding'). Ignore decorations like 'seen here' and 'VIDEO DAILY DOUBLE'.

edits.target: Do not talk yourself out of a well-supported entity.
edits.content: - A passage may quote the clue verbatim (J! Archive page, quiz blog, 'Quiz # Question' stub) WITHOUT showing the answer. Then the quote only confirms the clue is a trivia item. Take the answer from the encyclopedia, dictionary or news passages that match the clue's descriptors (e.g. 'Moscow park ... murders ... best-seller & film' -> the park the reviews name, 'Gorky Park'). Never answer 'not answerable' because the archive line lacks the answer.

edits.target: Brief reasoning belongs before the tags.
edits.content: - Naming clues ('It's what they call the unpasteurized milk', 'known as ...') want the full standard term, even when it contains the clue's noun ('raw milk'). The 'give only the missing part' rule applies when the clue shares a quoted hint word with the answer ('hasty' -> 'pudding'), not when the whole term is what is being named.

edits.target: Other named entities in the clue are anchors, never the answer.
edits.content:
- Exception for part-of-phrase and grammar clues ('The adverb in "think fast"', 'the verb in ...', 'the first word of ...'): the answer IS a word from the quoted phrase ('fast'). Pick the word that has the stated role.
- Two-definition clues joined by 'or' ('The mouth of the Mississippi or a Helen Reddy "Dawn"') work like crosswords: the answer is ONE word that satisfies both halves ('Delta'). Check each half against the passages and do not answer with just one half's entity.

edits.target: - Clue lists its own options ('Of North Park, East Park, West Park or South Park, it's where...'): the answer is exactly one of the listed options, copied verbatim. Use the context to pick which.
edits.content: - Set-completion clues ('The Trimurti consists of Brahma, Shiva & this one', 'Athos, Porthos & this musketeer'): the names in the clue are given. The answer is the remaining member of the group, the one the passages list next to those names every time ('Vishnu'). Never repeat a name already in the clue.
